blocks.raw: <Callout>The LEA does not expect architects to be licensed engineers in these systems. It expects architects to know enough to: (1) allocate appropriate space and clearances for equipment, (2) understand system requirements that affect building design, (3) verify compliance with applicable codes, and (4) communicate intelligently with the specialist engineers on their team.</Callout>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>The PEC follows the National Electrical Code (NEC) structure but with Philippine amendments. When a question specifies Philippine practice, always apply PEC, not NEC. The voltage levels differ: the US standard is 120/240V; the Philippine standard is 230/400V.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <Warn>RA 9514 is one of the most heavily tested Philippine laws across the entire LEA. It appears in both LEA-UTIL and in Laws and Professional Practice. Know the fire safety clearance process, the occupancy-based sprinkler requirements, the means of egress requirements, and the fire rating requirements for different elements of construction.</Warn>

Include: purpose, key components, governing code, critical design parameters, and one diagram (the system schematic or a typical riser diagram). These summaries become your rapid-review resource in the final weeks before the exam.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>Building Utilities is a subject where practice questions are particularly valuable. The scenarios are specific enough that reading theory alone does not build the problem-solving fluency the exam requires. Seek out past LEA questions, review board examination materials, and work through as many scenario-based utility problems as you can find.</Note>
